items.title: Aarti Pharmalabs , reading the 2026 Annual report and my thoughts and notes : 1) 9000MTPA Xanthine capacity now , largest Ex china and 3 rd largest gl...
items.description_html:
Aarti Pharmalabs , reading the 2026 Annual report and my thoughts and notes :

1) 9000MTPA Xanthine capacity now , largest Ex china and 3 rd largest globally with 15-20% Market share , after CPSC Group and Shandong in China

2) 21 CDMO customers , 35 commercial projects , 19 under development , below tweet have done my latest on the DMF tracker on where incremental filings are happening ( Aug-19 below tweet)
3) Employee count 2100 to 2400 this year , expect this to increase , we have seen some very good top level hiring in the research side from Aarti in this last quarter , lot of expertise in top talent has been added as per Pharma hiring trends
4) Capabilties : Continuous manufacturing, flow chemistry and bio-catalysis reaction, HPAPI (cytotoxic/oncology) and corticosteroids development and manufacturing, cryogenic reactors
5) R&D at 7.4% versus 5% Last year , 5 new patents filed this year , Dedicated block 2 at Atali planned for specific CDMO projects, with ground-breaking planned in Q3 FY 2026-27 and at a targeted completion within 12-15 months • R&D investment initiated in TIDES, including peptides and oligonucleotides, to expand long-term portfolio capabilitie

Again so far they are delivering well , this year there will be one quarter of new capex cost escalations to start kicking in so factor those costs in for maybe Q2 might be weaker , but if we remove that one cost step up function quarter , the next 2 years visibilty remains strong and trajectory is pivoting here , from API xanthine to CMDO tides as well

We have been tracking this story in detail , can refer to my older tweets as well from a year

disc : this is not investment advice/financial reccomendation , do your own due diligence , I am biased here from lower levels so take my opinion with salt and do your own research as well

items.title: RT The Arc: 🚨 Meesho has discontinued the role of chief product officer as part of a restructuring of its product organisation. Product leaders who...
items.description_html:
RT The Arc
🚨 Meesho has discontinued the role of chief product officer as part of a restructuring of its product organisation.

Product leaders who previously reported to CPO Prasanna Arunachalam will now report directly to their respective business heads.

Meesho said the change is intended to "strengthen accountability" and align "product strategy and execution with the long term needs of each business."

Arunachalam will no longer be classified as senior management personnel, although he will remain at the company.

Arunachalam was elevated to CPO in June 2025 after nearly five years at Meesho, where he previously led monetisation and content commerce.

He has about about 15 years of work experience at cos like online travel platform Cleartrip, advertising-tech company Vizury and Procter & Gamble.

items.title: Lot of people mistake calling a management good when it was actually sector tailwinds , and call a management bad when there is sectoral pain Both can...
items.description_html:
Lot of people mistake calling a management good when it was actually sector tailwinds , and call a management bad when there is sectoral pain

Both can be illusive , a track record of management always comes on how they handle a tough cycle and still emerge winners , thats why in many sectors with tailwinds there will be an illusion of management being very good because they are meeting guidance , following plans , but a lot of that is not them , it is the tailwind

Just note the difference , it is not the absolute truth , but one we should be mindful of creating a distinction

items.title: It may sound cringe but the learning is so critical here. I tried to make money in CPCL in last 3 cycles. And, always gave back all the gains. Given h...
items.description_html:
It may sound cringe but the learning is so critical here. I tried to make money in CPCL in last 3 cycles. And, always gave back all the gains. Given how the world was geopolitically changing, it was apparent that you'd need contra bets.
When you experice giving all gains back to market, you get over cautious and exit whenever you make a big return thinking what if it happens again. I did book CPCL once but re-entered only because of the past cycle experience. I could not enter some of the other stocks I exited. That's market for you.

If you aren't doing well or haven't done well, do not rush. Keep patience, you are subconciously soaking in the experience that will come to help eventually. It's a hidden compounding you seldom notice.

Same goes with Selan/Antelopus. For nearly 30 years, Selan held three highly valuable oilfields but failed to scale up. Production stagnated for nearly 20years! Investors were frustrated. I never made money in this one in past cycles. Failed to capitalize on new technology. Turnaround came in 2022 and stock went from 180cr mcap to 4000cr today.

I have countless examples from last 20yrs of my time in the market during which different set of investors called names to stock for not performing. Only to see those stocks being favorites of the street today. That gives me hope that if business capabilites are strong, companies make come back, always.


Ameya: Almost every 6 year, Chennai Petro falls to 80 odd level, rises to 460-480 and falls again to touch same level. It happened in 2009, happened in 2015, 2020 it just reversed from 80 and result also to assist!! Can we see cycle playing out again?

items.title: Global models are not “bad at Indic languages.” They are expensive at Hindi, Gujarati, Malayalam, Odia & so on. Tokenizers built for English and Chi...
items.description_html:
Global models are not “bad at Indic languages.”
They are expensive at Hindi, Gujarati, Malayalam, Odia & so on. Tokenizers built for English and Chinese fracture Indian scripts. You pay more tokens for the same sentence, burn more context, wait longer, and still lose accuracy on local exams, laws, and idioms.

Gnani claims to have rebuilt that tokenizer. Evon 3.3 uses about 20% fewer tokens per Indian-language word than the GPT-5 family tokenizer, and less than half what byte-level tokenizers in DeepSeek, Llama, and Qwen need.

It is lower inference cost, lower latency, and more usable context on the same GPU.

And the best part - It is designed to run on a single node (RTX 6000 Pro / L40S class), not an B200 or H200 cluster.


Ameya: Of these, Sarvam, Kore AI, Gnani AI seems to be doing well. While Murf, Skit and TWO seems to be in stress or have to pivot to survive, others, perhaps have gone into extreme niche or unable to find a killer use case.
Source: Gartner

items.title: A 2021 Deja Vu? Different Tightening, Same Deflationary Pressure China looks like 2021 again. The tightening is different. The deflation pressure isn...
items.description_html:
A 2021 Deja Vu? Different Tightening, Same
Deflationary Pressure

China looks like 2021 again. The tightening is different. The deflation pressure isn’t.

Different tightening. Same deflation trap.

• This is enforcement of existing rules - not another broad regulatory reset. Weak property and deflation risk limit how far Beijing can go.

• Official line: *4.7% is “realistic.”* Cleaning up LG debt, property and small banks *will cost growth.* Goods consumption is saturating; services have to do the work.

• Near-term job is deploying the *~Rmb2trn* already in the pipe. Extra easing stays in the toolkit, but *only if activity deteriorates further.*

• Why no rush: *high debt, diminishing investment returns, manufacturing overcapacity,* and a heavy *property inventory overhang.*

• Weak RMB is part of the *post-housing equilibrium* not a cheap-currency policy. A stronger yuan alone *doesn’t create the domestic demand China needs.*

*Bar for a major stimulus pivot still looks high.*

items.title: What is the ROIC on GenAI Capex? Everyone’s arguing about $1.5T of AI capex. The better question is the one almost nobody models: what’s the return?...
items.description_html:
What is the ROIC on GenAI Capex?

Everyone’s arguing about $1.5T of AI capex.

The better question is the one almost nobody models: what’s the return?

MS just published the first serious ROIC framework for GenAI. Their answer: paths to 25–50%.

They ran 1 GW of GB300-class capacity through 3 monetization models:

1. Hyperscaler GPU rental (IaaS)

AWS / Azure / GCP style
Revenue: ~$23bn per GW
Opex: ~$8bn (mostly IT depreciation)
Incremental EBIT margin: ~67%
After-tax: ~$12bn NOPAT
ROIC: ~31%

This is the “just rent the GPUs” business. Still very attractive.

2. Model API on owned infrastructure
The GOOGL / META / integrated-lab model
Revenue: ~$30bn per GW
Same ~$8bn cost base
Incremental EBIT margin: ~75%
ROIC: ~46%

Highest returns accrue to whoever owns both the model *and* the metal. Driven by inference mix, token throughput, and token pricing.

3. Model API on rented 3P compute
Higher revenue (~$40bn/GW) because of richer token pricing
But rental costs eat most of it (~$28bn)
Incremental margin compresses to ~31%
ROIC: ~25%

Still positive but the infrastructure owner captures a large share of the value.

MS’s conclusion: the best businesses in the Age of Inference won’t just be the ones spending the most. They’ll be the ones that control model + infrastructure.

That’s why they’re constructive on $AMZN $GOOGL $MSFT $META.

Capex is the headline. ROIC is the story.

items.description_html:
What are the biggest market dislocations? September 2026

Markets are still pricing Goldilocks. That landing zone is getting very thin.

4 dislocations that can’t last

• Fed: Shallow hike cycle still priced despite ISM services prices paid at a 4-year high — historically consistent with 5%+ CPI. Markets have underestimated hawkishness in 4 of the last 5 years.
• ECB: Hike pricing barely moved even as inflation swaps rose, gas jumped, and growth kept beating.
• Oil : Hormuz still blocked. Brent ~$96 vs the 6-month future at ~$83. Hopes of a fade keep getting dashed.
• Risk assets: Equities and credit remain complacent vs rising real yields and a cost-push shock. Easy rate cuts or fiscal rescue aren’t available this time.

Something has to give.

Persistent growth + limited inflation + modest hikes + fading supply shocks is an extremely narrow landing zone.

BREAKING: China’s central bank officially bought +20 tonnes of gold in August, matching its largest monthly purchase since October 2023.

This follows +20 tonnes and +15 tonnes acquired in July and June, respectively, and marks its 22nd consecutive monthly gold purchase.

So far in 2026, China has officially added +80 tonnes to its gold reserves, lifting total holdings to a record 2,387 tonnes.

By comparison, in full-year 2025, China increased its official gold reserves by a total of +29 tonnes.

In troy ounces, China added ~650,000 ounces to its reserves last month, taking its total holdings to a record 76.73 million ounces.

China continues to stockpile gold at a historic pace.

US high-grade corporate bond issuance is expected to surge to ~$215 billion in September, the largest September issuance on record.

This is set to surpass the previous September high of ~$205 billion, posted in 2025.

The current estimate is also more than triple the ~$70 billion issued in September 2022.

This follows $145.2 billion of US high-grade bonds issued in August, the highest August total on record, as AI-related data center buildouts continue to fuel corporate borrowing.

US companies have already borrowed more than $410 billion so far in 2026, specifically to fund data centers and other AI-related investments.

Meanwhile, retail investors have purchased more investment-grade bonds this year than in any full year in data going back to 2010.

The AI boom is driving a record corporate borrowing spree.

Average all-in sustaining cost (AISC) margins surged +134% YoY in Q1 2026, to a record $3,076 per ounce.

AISC margin is the amount miners earn per ounce of gold after covering the costs of sustaining their mining operations.

This is far above the +70% YoY increase in gold prices over the same period.

Furthermore, AISC margins among the 10% of gold miners with the highest production costs rose +32% QoQ, to $2,363 per ounce.

Since March 2024, global miner AISC margins have more than tripled, while gold prices have roughly doubled over the same period.

Gold miners are realizing massive profits.

items.title: RT Dr Y Nithiyanandam: A M4.9 earthquake struck Upper Mustang, Nepal, close to the Tibet frontier. USGS places it at 29.273°N, 83.978°E, with a prel...
items.description_html:
RT Dr Y Nithiyanandam
A M4.9 earthquake struck Upper Mustang, Nepal, close to the Tibet frontier. USGS places it at 29.273°N, 83.978°E, with a preliminary depth of 10 km.

What makes this event noteworthy is not the magnitude, but the location. This high-altitude border sector sees M~5 events less frequently than Nepal’s more active seismic zones.

The epicentre lies close to the Korala border corridor, connecting Upper Mustang with Tibet and, farther north, the wider road network around G219.

Worth watching: aftershocks, slope failures/rockfalls, the Korala–Lo Manthang road, border infrastructure, and any impacts reported from the Tibetan side.

⚠️ Location and depth remain preliminary and may be revised as seismic agencies review the event.

A moderate earthquake, but in a strategically and geologically interesting location.

#GEOINT #Nepal #Tibet #Earthquake #Himalayas #G219

items.title: Leading indicators point to higher US inflation. The ISM Services Prices Paid Index rose +2.3 points in August, to 72.6, its highest since July 2022. ...
items.description_html:
Leading indicators point to higher US inflation.

The ISM Services Prices Paid Index rose +2.3 points in August, to 72.6, its highest since July 2022.

Since February, the index has risen +9.6 points, its largest 6-month increase since May 2025.

Historically, this metric has led CPI inflation and core PCE inflation by ~6 months.

If the historical relationship holds, the current reading suggests CPI could rise to as high as 6.0% in the coming months, from 3.4% in July.

At the same time, this implies core PCE could increase above 4.0%, from July’s reported 3.3%.

Inflation pressures are intensifying in the US.

BREAKING: Copper prices on the LME have surged to a record $14,533 per ton, now up +47% over the last 12 months.

The surge comes amid a supply shortage with rising demand from data centers, renewable energy, and power grids.

Furthermore, expectations that President Trump will expand tariffs to refined copper imports have pushed US Comex prices above global prices.

This is encouraging traders to ship hundreds of thousands of tons of copper to the US this year to profit from the price difference.

Now, global stockpiles are increasingly concentrated in the US, draining LME inventories to critically low levels and leaving less copper readily available to buyers elsewhere.

Copper's supply crunch is accelerating.

items.title: What does a company making textile machinery have to do with fighter jets and rockets? Quite a lot, if that company knows how to innovate over time. C...
items.description_html:
What does a company making textile machinery have to do with fighter jets and rockets?

Quite a lot, if that company knows how to innovate over time.

Coimbatore-based Lakshmi Machine Works (LMW) started in 1962 as a textile machinery manufacturer. For decades, that was its core identity.

But instead of remaining confined to one industry, LMW took its engineering, machining and manufacturing capabilities into increasingly complex applications.

Nearly five decades later, it entered aerospace & defence.

Today, the same company that built textile machinery has contributed to programmes involving Tejas, Su-30, Hawk, Dornier, Boeing P-8I, DRDO and ISRO’s LVM3.

Think about that evolution:

Textile machinery → precision engineering → fighter aircraft → rockets 🚀

And LMW isn't stopping there.

It now plans to invest ₹1,050 Cr across aerospace, defence, and advanced manufacturing, potentially making these businesses a much bigger part of the company over time.

What I find fascinating is that LMW didn't abandon its original DNA.

The underlying DNA remained engineering + manufacturing.

It simply kept finding newer, more complex, and higher-value applications for those capabilities. That's perhaps one of the most underrated forms of innovation in business.

Innovation isn't always about inventing something new. Sometimes, it's about continuously reinventing where your existing capabilities can take you.

No stock reco.

RT Aditi Shrivastava
Swish's best kitchens push out 1,200 orders a day. A regular cloud kitchen manages 100-150.

That density is what investors are paying for. Swish has filed to raise Rs 224.54 crore in an extended Series B led by Bertelsmann India, valuing it at Rs 1,653 crore post-money - up over 30% from March.

From our deep dive on the economics: owning procurement, kitchens and delivery keeps food gross margins at 60-70%.

Indian Army -

CBRN Recce Vehicles – Specialised platforms used to detect, classify and track Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear contamination, while also marking affected zones. The platform originates from DRDO, with BEL receiving ToT for the tracked Mk-II version in June 2025. Potential beneficiaries: BEL and AVNL.

High Mobility Vehicles (HMVs) – Heavy-duty mobility platforms designed to move personnel, equipment and supplies across demanding terrain. Procurement is competitive, with BEML, Tata Motors and Ashok Leyland among established suppliers to the Army.

Self-Propelled Mechanical Mine Layers (MMLs) – Mechanised systems that enable rapid deployment of minefields across challenging terrain. The programme has a DRDO technology lineage.

Advanced Light Helicopters (ALH) – Additional requirements for the indigenous Dhruv helicopter, for which HAL is the sole-source manufacturer.
Trawl Tanks – Armoured mine-clearing systems used to breach minefields and create safe passages for advancing combat formations. Based on DRDO-developed technology; BEML has an established presence in tank-based mine-clearing systems.

Sarvatra Bridge System – Mobile military bridging equipment capable of deploying a 75-metre multi-span bridge, mounted on an 8×8 high-mobility platform. BEML is the production agency.

Indian Navy -

Arudhra Radars – Indigenous 4D active phased-array medium-power radars intended to replace legacy air-surveillance radars deployed at naval aviation bases. Developed by DRDO, with BEL a likely beneficiary.

Marine Gas Turbines (MGT) – Focus on developing an indigenous gas-turbine propulsion system for Indian warships, followed by procurement once development is completed. The programme could reduce India's reliance on imported naval propulsion technology.

Indian Air Force

Fighter, Transport & Helicopter Capability – Procurement aimed at strengthening the IAF's combat aviation, airlift and rotary-wing capabilities.

Ground-Based Multi-Purpose Jammer (GBMPJ) – Electronic-warfare equipment designed to disrupt and degrade hostile radar systems. The vendor has not been specified; BEL is an established production partner for several DRDO-developed ground-based EW systems.

Defence Forces Secure Access Card (DEFSAC) – A common RFID-based smart identity and access system intended to digitise and replace physical identity cards, entry passes and permits across defence establishments.

items.title: The ₹6 lakh crore that "vanished" from India's GDP It didn't vanish. SBI Research's new Ecowrap says the full ₹42 lakh crore revision got re-measure...
items.description_html:
The ₹6 lakh crore that "vanished" from India's GDP

It didn't vanish. SBI Research's new Ecowrap says the full ₹42 lakh crore revision got re-measured, not erased, and the math is simpler than the outrage.

What the report actually shows:

- Nominal GDP was cut ₹41.8 lakh crore across Q1 FY23 to Q2 FY26. That is 4.1% of GDP over those 14 quarters, not a hole in the economy.

- Real GDP over the same window was raised ₹372 lakh crore. Lower nominal with higher real means prices came off, not output. Same goods, lower prices.

- 95% of the cut sits in one bucket: Trade, Hotels, Transport and Communication, down ₹39 lakh crore. Finance, Insurance, Real Estate and Business Services moved the other way, up ₹13.6 lakh crore.

- The reason is method, not manipulation. The FY23 series measures the informal economy directly using ASUSE and PLFS survey data instead of proxies, so activity got re-sorted between sectors.

- Revisions are routine: 239 over 70 quarters since FY09, 134 up and 105 down, with no pattern by government.

Key takeaway: the "missing" number is a measurement upgrade, not a disappearing act. Focus on the logic, not the print.

Caveat: this is SBI's own rebuttal in a live, politically charged debate. Anyone who distrusts the base-year switch will read the same revision differently.

items.title: RT Ananth Rupanagudi: Late 1940s, Calcutta (Kolkata) - View of Lindsay Street, courtesy Bombay Photo Stores Ltd, Calcutta. Lindsay Street in Kolkata (...
items.description_html:
RT Ananth Rupanagudi
Late 1940s, Calcutta (Kolkata) - View of Lindsay Street, courtesy Bombay Photo Stores Ltd, Calcutta. Lindsay Street in Kolkata (formerly Calcutta) is a historic commercial thoroughfare best known for housing the iconic New Market (Sir Stuart Hogg Market).

The street was originally named after Robert Lindsay, a British colonial officer who arrived in India in 1776 and served as the collector of Dhaka in 1777. In July 1978, the road was officially renamed Nellie Sengupta Sarani to honour the prominent freedom fighter and second European woman to lead the Indian National Congress. Nellie Sengupta was an Englishwoman who married Bengali nationalist leader Jatindramohan Sengupta and dedicated her life to India's independence movement.

Bombay Photo Stores (often abbreviated as BPS) is an iconic institutional name in the history of commercial photography in Kolkata. Founded in 1948, it was situated at the historic 33 & 34 Park Mansion on Park Street, anchoring it directly in the city's premium lifestyle and commercial district.

At its operational peak, the studio's legacy was deeply tied to the passionate photographer and businessman Jayant Patel. He owned and operated three prominent studios alongside a massive photo-processing laboratory under the BPS umbrella. Patel famously balanced commercial success with an artistic passion for street photography, documenting daily life in the city from the 1940s through the 1970s. #Kolkata #streets #history @somnath1978 @TheRightGhose

items.description_html:
US homebuyers are walking away from deals at the highest rate in years:

14.0% of home-purchase agreements that went under contract fell through in July, the highest rate since November 2023.

The national cancellation rate has held between 13.0% and 14.0% over the last 4 years, well above the lower rates typical of the seller's market from 2020 to 2022.

Atlanta posted the highest cancellation rate last month, at 19.8%, followed by Houston at 19.6%, San Antonio at 18.7%, and Las Vegas at 18.6%.

This comes as sellers outnumber buyers by ~51%, near the highest percentage on record, giving buyers more options and making them more willing to walk away over inspection issues, low appraisals, or rejected concessions.

At the same time, high home prices and elevated mortgage rates are leaving buyers with less financial room, making unexpected costs or concerns about taking on large monthly payments more likely to derail deals.

The housing market is under historic pressure.

items.title: RT menaka doshi: India Realty Check The upcoming festive season in India will be a test for the country’s red-hot real estate market, which is alread...
items.description_html:
RT menaka doshi
India Realty Check

The upcoming festive season in India will be a test for the country’s red-hot real estate market, which is already showing signs of moderating demand.

The post-pandemic housing boom has run into rising construction costs, expensive land and increasingly stretched homebuyers, shows data from Anarock Research.

Average construction costs for standard and premium residential projects are up 34% since 2021, while land prices have risen 50% to 120% across the top seven cities over that period.

Combined with location premiums and developer margins, rising home prices, up 59% in that period, present an “urgent affordability crisis for buyers,” the Anarock report says.

After Covid, the rush to build premium projects has driven land to peak prices, Dr. Prashant Thakur, director and head of research and advisory at Anarock, tells me. For a few years, demand more than matched supply. Until a few quarters ago, projects could sell out almost immediately after launch because of the FOMO factor among buyers.

That fear of missing out has faded, except for a few projects and neighborhoods.

Geopolitical tensions, AI-related job concerns, weaker equity markets and rising home prices have made buyers more cautious, Thakur says. There’s no obvious trigger right now to recreate the buying frenzy of the past few years.

Read India Edition
https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2026-09-07/india-s-housing-boom-faces-a-festive-season-test?srnd=undefined

items.description_html:
After the $ deluge comes the ₹ flood.

While one might assume, its easier to deal with the latter, its not so easy after all.

💸Banks, naturally, want the option that is best for them. So they seem to have pushed the idea of long term VRRRs (variable rate reverse repo auctions used to withdraw funds mostly for short term).

💸BUT they claim its too difficult for them to forecast liquidity for any length of time (certainly not 30 days) because of 24X7 RTGS etc (difficult to believe btw). So they wanted a VRRR with an early withdrawal options.

💸Well, the RBI gave in and they still didn't manage to take out the 7 trillion rupees (which was the amount for VRR). Banks just didn't subscribe. So the RBI did a shorter VRRR.

💸It seems like the solution here has to be a more blunt tool where the surplus liquidity is sequestered (given inflation is already rising). Between OMOs/CRR and (the most preferred by banks) FX swaps. MSS/CMB - when RBI has tools why go to the govt?

Views?

items.title: Does the RBI even need to sterilize the FCNR based inflows? I'm coming to the conclusion the answer is probably no. When RBI creates money by printing...
items.description_html:
Does the RBI even need to sterilize the FCNR based inflows? I'm coming to the conclusion the answer is probably no.

When RBI creates money by printing rupees to buy dollars, the way its done for the FCNR swap, banks have a lot of money with the RBI. The money with the RBI stays with the RBI - it only moves from one bank to the other (or the government).

Whatever banks need for CRR is sequestered away by banks, so the excess liquidity then is placed back into the RBI as reverse repo.

Why would liquidity at the RBI be a problem? If banks were net borrowers from the RBI, then RBI printing has an inflationary impact, perhaps, by reducing borrowing cost due to more supply. That is not the case even before the FCNR, as banks have had excess liquidiyt for a while.

If this excess liquidity causes RBI to pay like 5.25% for it in INR (to banks on reverse repo, that is kinda sorta offset by the 4.4% the RBI earns in dollars for the $127bn reserves they have to keep to return that FCNR. So there's no major impact on RBI accounts.

Will banks go crazy lending? They can't; they will creat NPAs if they go bonkers, and that will destroy their capital. Their capital ratios determine how much their lending can grow. That is not linked with RBI printing money, so banks have net parked excesses with RBI because they don't want to lend beyond capital ratio allowances.

Should the government issue bonds to sterilize, like they did in 2005? No. That time, banks were net borrowers from RBI and inflation was a distinct possibility, so the government did MSS bonds. Not needed now - it moves the interest cost to the govt (deficit increases, inflation increases) but RBI is the one that earns the interest on the USD. Then if people like me say that RBI should pay all those profits back to the government, all the uncles gets full on foaming at the mouth. So let it stay with the RBI (which should anyhow pay any of the profits earned to the govt)

(Note: I first wrote about RBI needing to pay as much as 300,000 cr. as dividends in December 2018. https://premium.capitalmind.in/2018/12/abeyaar-rbi-is-hoarding-too-much-capital-and-can-pay-a-chunk-to-the-government/
After that the govt got paid 1.76 lakh cr as dividends, then after four years of denials, the RBI is now paying more than 2 lakh crores a year to the govt.)

So sterlization isn't necessary and distorts the govt accounts unnecessarily.

items.description_html:
RT Anushka Saxena
Delighted to share my latest Issue Brief for @TakshashilaInst, 'China’s Taiwan Tryst and The 2027 Question: Military Scenarios and Operational Realities'.

https://takshashila.org.in/content/publications/China-Taiwan-2027-20260903.html

In the run-up to the PLA’s centenary in August 2027 and the 21st Party Congress in October 2027, the 2027 timeline has been widely misread. This Brief finds that:

- For Beijing, 2027 is a capability milestone rather than a campaign date. The American alarmist reading, delivered alongside budget advocacy, has since been walked back by the US’s intelligence community itself.
- Across three PLA offensive campaign options, Beijing’s roadmap can best be understood as a coercion ladder designed to win without landing on the island. Its binding constraints, in this regard, are troop sustainment and port access, and not the initial landing.
- Chinese pressure on the LAC during a Taiwan contingency is plausible, but inducement – including the proposition for Early Harvest boundary settlement – may buy Indian acquiescence.

Check out the full paper, which also includes a section on three types of campaigns Beijing may pursue vis-à-vis Taiwan, my assessments of the implications of such a campaign for India, and a discussion of decisive platforms for the PLA’s amphibious lift and beaching endeavours in a Taiwan campaign.

items.title: RT 𑀓𑀺𑀭𑀼𑀱𑁆𑀡𑀷𑁆 🇮🇳: More than 1,000 years later, Rajaraja Chola continues to speak to us through stone. A previously und...
items.description_html:
RT 𑀓𑀺𑀭𑀼𑀱𑁆𑀡𑀷𑁆 🇮🇳
More than 1,000 years later, Rajaraja Chola continues to speak to us through stone.

A previously undocumented inscription of the great Chola emperor has now been discovered at the Vedapureeswarar Temple at Therazhundur, Mayiladuthurai.

Dated to Rajaraja’s 18th regnal year (c. 1003 CE), it records an endowment of 21 kalanju of gold to the Mahasabha of Tiruvazhundur (Therazhundur), a Brahmadeya in Uyyakondar Valanadu. The Mahasabha was to invest the gold and use the interest earned from the endowment to provide food offerings (amudu) to the deity Tirukkadavudai Nayanar.

What looks like a simple temple donation actually tells us much more, about Chola territorial administration, the functioning of village Mahasabhas, management of permanent endowments and the economic role of temples.

Pic courtesy: Dinamalar

items.title: The Non Auto Pivot taking place in Sundram Fasteners Sundram Fasteners is trying to shift its revenue mix away from Indian auto OEM fasteners and powe...
items.description_html:
The Non Auto Pivot taking place in Sundram Fasteners

Sundram Fasteners is trying to shift its revenue mix away from Indian auto OEM fasteners and powertrain parts (which is the bulk of its ~₹6,000 cr book) into three engineered-product lines that sell to non-auto customers:

Wind: turbine fasteners and precision parts, already the biggest of the three at ₹25–30 cr/month (350 cr annualised). Management is building capacity to ₹500 cr with only 100 cr of capex.

Aerospace: 50 cr in FY26, targeted at 100 cr+ in FY27 and 500 cr in 2–3 years.

Railways: 2–3 cr/month today, target is 100 cr annual.

Why they are doing it?

Margins: Wind, aero and rail parts are lower-volume, qualification-heavy and priced on engineering rather than on annual OEM cost-downs. They carry structurally better margins than commodity fasteners to Maruti or Tata.

De-cyclicalisation: Domestic auto is cyclical, and a large chunk of Sundram's existing book is ICE powertrain (engine fasteners, pump assemblies, cold-forged parts) that faces slow erosion as EV penetration rises. Wind and rail run on infrastructure/energy capex cycles that are uncorrelated with car demand; aerospace runs on a multi-year global backlog.

Capital efficiency: The wind division will have sales potential of 500 cr post 100 cr capex. Management is using the existing forging and machining base to add new end-markets rather than building greenfield.

Global customer diversification: Wind and aerospace customers are largely global OEMs, which also helps the export mix and reduces reliance on a handful of domestic auto accounts.

Disclaimer: no reco to buy or sell. Even elephants can dance and change the product mix eventually :)

items.title: The Next Cycle Isn’t Just Chips JPM’s Sept 2026 Global Markets Outlook isn’t another “buy AI” note. It’s a map of the physical and local constra...
items.description_html:
The Next Cycle Isn’t Just Chips

JPM’s Sept 2026 Global Markets Outlook isn’t another “buy AI” note. It’s a map of the physical and local constraints that will actually decide the next investment cycle:

• Compute stays scarce - old-GPU rental rates remain sticky, hyperscalers keep raising capex, SPE order books are only just turning. If AI is existential, semi spend still has a long way to go.
• Power is the new staple - the bottleneck is electrons, not models. Grid capex is exploding, Asia is quietly re-rating nuclear, and Korea power-equipment backlogs are already screaming.
• Robotics goes exponential - China industrial robot volumes are re-accelerating. Humanoids are moving from R&D curiosity into industrial + logistics use-cases on a multi-year S-curve.
• Defense umbrella expands - mil-spend/GDP is rising across India, Korea, Japan, Taiwan. Korea export orders are inflecting; India production is scaling. This is multi-year, not a one-cycle trade.
• Asia localizes - markets with lower foreign trading share look more resilient if dollar/flows get ugly. Households still sit in property + deposits; onshore volumes have already structurally lifted.

The last cycle was software + cheap money.

The next one is compute, power, robots, defense, and domestic buyers.

items.description_html:
RT Normal Guy
RBI put 15-year cap on how long bank CEOs can stay Also set age limit at 70

Promoter CEOs get only 12 years, These rules forced out Aditya Puri from HDFC Bank after 26 years in 2020. Uday Kotak left Kotak Mahindra Bank in 2023. Both banks ran smoothly under long-serving founders. After they left, HDFC Bank has already gone through messy governance fights and its second CEO Jagdishan is now leaving.

Kotak hired Ashok Vaswani from Barclays, and he quit within 3 years, Forced turnover creates instability

When private banks cannot find CEOs internally, they turn to retired PSU bankers. RBL Bank got Subramaniakumar, former head of Indian Overseas Bank. Stock fell 22% on that announcement day in 2022.

Bandhan Bank got Partha Sengupta, also from Indian Overseas Bank and SBI. HDFC Bank itself now has its 3rd IAS officer serving as part-time chairman. Rajiv Kumar joined that role in 2026.

Private banks were built to be different from government-run lenders. Now their leadership pools look increasingly similar that distinction is fading.

No major Indian private bank has had smooth CEO handover in recent years. HDFC Bank CEO Jagdishan is leaving Oct 2026 after governance issues and board fights with former chairman Chakraborty.

Kotak CEO Vaswani lasted under 3 years before citing personal reasons to leave in Dec 2026. IndusInd CEO Kathpalia resigned over $230mn accounting mess. Before that, RBL Bank saw its CEO exit under regulator pressure.

Investors paid premium prices for these stocks expecting stable leadership. Every surprise exit chips away at that premium.

RBI need to be better + flexible & if this not change then things will continue and now Private bank have now PSU competition because the mess of PSU is now gone too + that edge is narrow

items.title: Example of how manufacturing companies climb the value chain: Loose components to sub assemblies to integrated systems and finally in some cases to Mi...
items.description_html:
Example of how manufacturing companies climb the value chain:

Loose components to sub assemblies to integrated systems and finally in some cases to Mission critical industrial solutions, (Aerospace, Defence etc)

Climbing the value chain means the company stops selling a part and starts selling a solved problem.

Step 1: Loose components (needle/cylindrical bearings). Here the product is a catalogue item. The customer's purchasing team compares your bearing against five others on price and delivery. You're paid roughly per kilo of steel converted, competition includes Chinese imports, switching cost is close to zero, and margins get squeezed the moment steel prices move. Volumes are large but the business is a price-taker.

Step 2: Sub-assemblies (wheel hubs, steering components). Now you're combining bearings, housing, seals, sensors into one unit that bolts straight onto the vehicle. Two things change: the customer saves assembly labour and quality risk, so they'll pay for that, and the part is designed into a specific vehicle platform. Once you're on the drawing, you supply for the platform's 6–8 year life. Switching becomes painful for the OEM, so pricing power improves and revenue visibility lengthens.

Step 3: Integrated systems (complete friction/motion solutions). The customer stops specifying the product and starts specifying the outcome — "I need this axle to carry X load at Y rpm for Z hours." You own the engineering, the testing, and the IP. This turns you from a vendor into a development partner who sits in the OEM's design meetings two years before launch. Content per vehicle rises sharply (you're capturing value that used to go to the OEM's own engineers), gross margins expand, and competition shrinks to a handful of global players who can do the same.

Step 4: Cross-industry platforms (aerospace, mission-critical industrial). The same core competence i.e. precision, metallurgy, reliability under stress is redeployed into markets where failure is catastrophic and price is secondary. Qualification cycles run 3–5 years, so once you're in, you're effectively an incumbent for decades. Margins are the highest, and critically, you're no longer hostage to the auto cycle. Diversified end-markets smooth earnings and earn a higher multiple from investors.

What it adds up to across the four steps:

1. Pricing basis shifts from cost-plus to value-based.
2. Margins expand and become more stable.
3. Customer relationships lengthen from purchase orders to multi-year platforms.
4. Competitive set shrinks from dozens to a few.
5. Capital intensity and R&D rise, but return on that capital rises faster.
6. Earnings become less cyclical and the market re-rates the business.

Study businesses like Sona BLW or Cumi or NRB with this lens. How companies climb the value chain in manufacturing will become clearer!

Disc: no reco to buy or sell.

items.description_html:
Diagnostic index is moving to new all time highs

The Four Macro Drivers Behind the Index Rally (as per the Q1FY27 calls of the companies in this space)

1) Pricing has rationalized, restoring realizations

> Discounting fatigue is visible across management commentary. Lal PathLabs says there's been "no structural price change" over the last few quarters and pricing is "neither too favorable nor deteriorating".
> Metropolis hasn't taken a single price hike in 18 months (last increase January 2025) yet still grew realizations 5–6% purely from mix, suggesting price competition has stopped eroding revenue.
> Suraksha explicitly avoids deep discounting in its B2C collection centres; Vijaya's last price hike was a limited Hyderabad-only one in June 2025

2) Volume + mix, not price, is the growth engine

> Q1 FY27 volume growth was broad-based: Lal PathLabs patients +8.2%, Metropolis test volumes +11%, Vijaya test volumes +16.5%, Thyrocare pathology volumes +28%, Suraksha tests +11%.
> Wellness and preventive testing is the premiumization lever. Organised players' wellness revenue has grown at ~25% CAGR over 5 years and now contributes roughly 12–25% of revenue. Vijaya's pure wellness mix hit 14.8% vs ~8% pre-COVID; Lal PathLabs' Swasthfit bundle is 27% of revenue growing ~20%.
> Tier 2/3 expansion is the structural volume story. Metropolis believes the small-town healthcare buildout "will continue for the next at least 2 decades". Suraksha and Krsnaa are both expanding aggressively beyond their home markets

3) Operating leverage is restoring margins

> OPMs now span 24.7% (Metropolis) to 42.7% (Vijaya), with the integrated radiology-plus-pathology and B2C-heavy models at the top. Vijaya expanded margins 360 bps YoY on 22.8% revenue growth; Lal PathLabs' OPM hit 31.0% (a four-year-high growth quarter); Suraksha's inflected to ~34.7% as new centres turned profitable.

4) Regulatory tailwind: CGHS/ECHS rate revision

> CGHS (Central Government Health Scheme) rate hikes are adding 2–3% at Lal PathLabs' company level, flowing straight to margin, expected to persist another 2–3 quarters. Suraksha got a ~1.5% top-line benefit; Metropolis barely benefits (~1% CGHS exposure). Krsnaa sees no immediate benefit since tender rates are contractually fixed, but future tenders may reset higher.

items.title: #DPIAlert | SoftBank and Alpha Wave have monetised stakes worth about Rs 2,200 crore ($233 mn) through their latest sales. But the outcomes are sharpl...
items.description_html:
#DPIAlert | SoftBank and Alpha Wave have monetised stakes worth about Rs 2,200 crore ($233 mn) through their latest sales. But the outcomes are sharply different.

Meesho: SoftBank sold about 1.7% for Rs 1,650 crore. It did not participate in Meesho’s IPO OFS, making this its first reported cash-out from the company.

SoftBank first invested in Meesho in 2021, at a valuation of $2.1 billion. The company’s current market capitalisation stands at about $10 billion.

Broadly, the latest sale translates into an estimated return of at least 4-5x.

Its remaining stake of roughly 6.9% is worth about Rs 6,500 crore.

Pine Labs: Alpha Wave sold nearly its entire 3.1% stake for about Rs 550 crore. The firm did not sell shares in the IPO, making this its first major liquidity event in Pine Labs.

Alpha Wave invested in Pine Labs at the peak of the funding boom in 2022, at a valuation of $5 billion.

With its current market capitalisation hovering around $2 billion, the investment translates into a loss of about 50%.

items.title: RT Prabhu, CEO, Fibocan: Re Thank you Prashant. Please stress this point if are in any high level meeting with SEBI and other stakeholders 1. Expiring...
items.description_html:
RT Prabhu, CEO, Fibocan
Re Thank you Prashant. Please stress this point if are in any high level meeting with SEBI and other stakeholders

1. Expiring day F&O traders should be settled at 15.15 price ( no need to build any additional 30 minutes vWAP for managing it. Jus the simple LTP (Last traded price) can be used as a reference price for settling options 2. Living or open F&O contracts can be allowed to trade between 15.20 till 15.40 as the case is now 3. To make CAS a realistic Equilibrium price discovery mechanism, the CAS price cannot be more than + or - 0.30% ( Yes less than half a percent) from the 15.15 traded price. This will ensure there is no undue manipulation and hence less of volatility 4. Manage by Exceptions - In the rarest of rare cases ( ie when "Unknown Unknown Risk" where there is some major news flow that has come in which has the potential to impact the price, then SEBI can direct exchanges open another window between 15.30 to 15.33 where the price movement can be allowed by another 2% on either side. If still the news is such a breaking one ( like announcement of lock down), another 3 minute window can be allowed, where in normal circuit breaker can be introduced ( whatever circuit level currently set in) 5. Please note that this exception is like Emergency exit and should be triggered only on the "Rarest of the Rare Cases" ( occurrence of Unknown Unknown Risk situation) only

items.description_html:
Ather Energy: Building A Scalable EV Platform Beyond Premium Scooters

Ather is transitioning from a premium electric scooter maker into a broader EV mobility platform by expanding its product portfolio, manufacturing capacity, distribution network and software ecosystem.

Key Strategic Progress

1. Product Portfolio Expansion

Expanded beyond the core 450 platform with Rizta S (159 km) and Rizta S (161 km) variants.
Rizta has become Ather’s fastest-selling product, strengthening its presence in the family scooter segment.
Upcoming EL platform and e-bike portfolio could expand its addressable market beyond scooters.

2. Geographic Expansion

Replicated its South India success model in new markets.
Middle India market share increased from 4.1% in Q1 FY25 to 17.4% in Q4 FY26.
The company is now scaling this playbook across the rest of India through stronger retail and service presence.

3. Distribution & Service Network Scale-Up

Retail and service network doubled during FY26.
Wider footprint improves customer accessibility and supports faster adoption in new regions.

4. Manufacturing Scale-Up

Factory 3.0 development is progressing, with Phase 1 targeting 5 lakh units annual capacity.
Upon completion of both phases, combined manufacturing capacity across Hosur and Factory 3.0 is expected to reach 14.2 lakh units annually.
Increased localisation of components like transmission, electronics and painting can improve cost efficiency and supply-chain resilience.

5. Software-Led Revenue Opportunity

AtherStack Pro achieved 91% attach rate in FY26.
Software and digital services are becoming an additional revenue stream, improving customer lifetime value.

6. Margin Improvement & Operating Leverage

Gross margin, EBITDA margin and profitability improved through:
Higher operating leverage
Better cost discipline
Scale benefits

Investment Perspective
Ather’s next phase is not just about selling more scooters — it is about building a vertically integrated EV ecosystem.

The key factors to track:

EL platform adoption

Factory 3.0 ramp-up

Expansion beyond South India

Improvement in margins

Growth of software-led revenues

If execution remains strong, Ather could evolve from a niche premium EV player into a scaled EV technology company with multiple growth engines.

I agree, I don't understand the issue against manufacturing or chip making. It is when you make that you accidently or pointedly discover what more can be made. Just moving defence imports to local manufacturing helped us make much more in drone and other equipment.

We already have people that can design chips. Then make them too, it's a leap that's taken much capital in the past and for the first time we have adequate domestic capital.

We need to make things. Not import 95% of our umbrellas. Or all our sewing machines. Just reducing imports by making more means so much more.

We need to explore our oil reserves. Our gold reserves. Make thorium work for us. Change energy to mostly self sourced, make things for India and so on.

We do need to reduce red tape and allow for more labour reform, etc. And cut corruption much more.


Prasanna Viswanathan: Long interview. Besides his usual tirade against industrial policy, which by now sounds increasingly hollow, Raghuram Rajan's reasoning for criticising India’s semiconductor mission is particularly bizarre.

Chips, he argues, are “the most easily smuggled thing on earth.”

items.title: Long time since I posted here. Not because of markets. The technology, the process, and the conversations around both have been moving so fast that I ...
items.description_html:
Long time since I posted here.

Not because of markets. The technology, the process, and the conversations around both have been moving so fast that I had to choose. Focus. Realign. Reskill. Build.

In my line of work, that felt like the only honest move. The last 6–8 months were really hard. Loss of my FIL who was as close to me as my father, markets punishing bullish bets wore down hard.

I love to build. When I do, it helps me heal. Different people, different ways of coping. I was also wrong on some bets, and that stung.

Hard lesson for me: don’t put your neck out for a business or a person you haven’t known long enough. Show conviction in position size, not in posts. I learned that the expensive way.

One of the bigger lessons: the worst mistakes are often made in the best of times.

Looking back over the last two years, most of what I’m paying for today was done during the bullish phase back 2yrs ago. I trusted people. I took management at their word. I didn’t force a third perspective hard enough.

Bullishness clouded judgment on a few fronts. That’s not usually how I operate. This time the reasoning went quiet, and I missed things I should have seen. The intent was never bad. I still hold the positions. What wore me down was the DMs, the name-calling, the cheap shots. I thought I have lost the trust of those who looked up to me. For a while that made posting here feel pointless.

This isn’t the first time I’ve been against the wall. Every time I’ve been pushed into a corner, I’ve come back by doing the work.

The last six months were that: a lot of agentic systems, harnesses, and observability built inside the enterprise. Quiet work. Deeply satisfying. I’ll keep posting the things that matter. There are still enough people here who value the perspective and see beyond stocks and price points. That’s enough for me. I do not seek a reply or a like, just sharing a heartfelt message here. Cheers. Keep building.

At #CareEdgeConversations, industry leaders Mr Ajendra Kumar Agarwal, CMD, @GRInfraprojects; Mr Samuel Joseph, Deputy Managing Director, National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development @NaBFID_official; and Mr Gaurav Chandna, Executive Director & Joint CEO, Vertis Infrastructure Trust; shared their perspectives on the next phase of India’s infrastructure growth.

Moderated by @RevatiKasture, Executive Director, CareEdge Ratings, the conversation explored some of the key priorities shaping the road ahead:

🔹 Long-term infrastructure planning over short-term interventions

🔹 Logistics parks and supply-chain infrastructure as the next major growth opportunity

🔹 Better integration of road, rail, and logistics networks

🔹 Innovative financing and greater mobilisation of private capital

🔹 The growing role of InvITs, bond markets, and alternative financing models

🔹 Addressing challenges around land availability, connectivity, and execution

The larger message was clear: India has built significant infrastructure scale. The next challenge, and opportunity, is to make that infrastructure more integrated, efficient, and competitive.

India’s energy transition is no longer just about adding renewable capacity, it is about building an ecosystem that can deliver energy security, reliability and sustainable growth.

At #CareEdgeConversations, industry leaders Mr Kuldeep Jain, Founder & MD, @CleanMax_Ofc; Mr Sandeep Lakhanpal, Managing Director, @JHargrett49946; Mr Kailash Vaswani, CFO, ReNew Energy Global PLCC; and Mr Abishek Pareek, CFO, Waaree Group came together to discuss what lies ahead for India’s energy transition.

Moderated by Sachin Gupta, ED and CRO, CareEdge Ratings, the conversation highlighted some of the critical priorities shaping the next phase:

🔹 Transmission infrastructure needs to keep pace with the rapid addition of renewable capacity.

🔹 Renewables + storage are increasingly becoming commercially competitive with conventional power.

🔹 Supply-chain resilience and backward integration will be critical to India’s energy security.

🔹 Domestic solar manufacturing has significant potential, but scale, technology, and cost competitiveness remain key.

🔹 Capital availability remains strong, particularly for robust projects, while access to debt needs continued attention.

🔹 The C&I renewable energy segment is witnessing rapid growth, opening up significant opportunities for developers.

🔹 Ultimately, India's transition will require an integrated ecosystem spanning generation, transmission, storage, manufacturing, and finance.

The message was clear: India’s renewable journey is entering a more complex but significantly larger phase, one where energy transition and energy security must move together.

items.description_html:
Ashutosh Fibre IPO : A Technical Yarn Player Moving Towards Higher-Value Products

Ashutosh Fibre is an interesting play on technical textiles rather than conventional textile demand. The company manufactures specialised yarns engineered for specific performance characteristics such as high tensile strength, flame resistance, heat resistance, chemical stability, abrasion resistance and anti-static properties.

Its products ultimately find applications across defence, protective clothing, automotive components, filtration and pollution control, geotextiles, industrial fabrics, thermal insulation, packaging and home furnishing.

Why the Business Looks Interesting

1. The biggest change is happening in the revenue mix and profitability.

Revenue from operations increased only modestly from Rs. 109.9 crore in FY24 to Rs. 117.4 crore in FY26, but EBITDA increased from Rs. 16.1 crore to Rs. 31.1 crore over the same period.

As a result:

EBITDA margin: 14.7% → 15.6% → 26.5%
PAT: Rs. 7.0 crore → Rs. 8.5 crore → Rs. 16.0 crore
PAT margin: 6.4% → 7.5% → 13.7%
ROCE: 21.0% → 16.3% → 26.3%

So FY26 growth was less about topline acceleration and more about a sharp improvement in business mix and profitability.

The most interesting development is the shift away from Indutech towards higher-growth categories.

2. What Industries Does It Serve?

Its yarn portfolio gives it exposure to several specialised applications:

Protech: Flame-retardant and heat-resistant yarns used in PPE, safety apparel and industrial thermal barriers.

Mobiltech: Friction-resistant yarns used in brake pads, clutch facings and transmission components.

Indutech: Filtration, filter cartridges, ropes, webbings and other industrial applications.

Hometech: Home furnishing textiles, carpets and filtration media.

Its broader product range includes para-aramid-based spun yarn, high-tenacity polyester, meta-aramid, FR viscose, modacrylic yarn, polypropylene yarn, stainless-steel yarn and specialised friction-spun yarns.
That creates exposure to structural themes including industrial safety, defence, automotive, pollution control and filtration, infrastructure and specialised manufacturing.

3. Capacity Is Becoming The Next Constraint

The company's main technical/synthetic yarn capacity stood at 3,750 MT in FY26, while production reached 3,619 MT.

That means utilisation has increased sharply:

FY24: 80.2%
FY25: 86.6%
FY26: 96.5%

This is important because the existing facility is approaching full utilisation precisely when newer categories such as Protech are scaling.

Ashutosh Fibre therefore plans to expand within its existing Petlad, Gujarat facility, adding compact spinning systems and high-value yarn attachments such as the Pinter Hard Core system.

Expanding within the existing facility should allow the company to leverage existing infrastructure, workforce and administrative resources — potentially making the expansion more capital-efficient.
Moving Downstream Into Modacrylic Fabrics
Another interesting strategy is forward integration.

4. Moving up in Value Chain
Ashutosh already manufactures modacrylic-based yarn used for high-performance fabrics. It now wants to move into manufacturing and selling the fabric itself.

The company has started trial production through third-party weaving and processing facilities and is targeting approximately 20,000 metres of modacrylic-based fabric sales per month.

The important part is that Ashutosh's own yarn would be consumed as the raw material.

This potentially allows it to move from being only a yarn supplier towards a higher-value finished technical textile product, improving value addition and potentially margins.

5. Exports Could Become Another Growth Lever

Exports are already meaningful:

FY24: Rs. 47.9 crore — 43.6% of revenue
FY25: Rs. 43.4 crore — 38.1%
FY26: Rs. 45.8 crore — 39.0%

The company plans to use additional capacity to target new international markets for specialised technical yarns.

Ashutosh Fibre is interesting because three transitions are happening simultaneously:

Volume → Value: Higher-value technical and performance yarns are becoming more important.

Yarn → Fabric: The company is attempting to move downstream into modacrylic technical fabrics.

Domestic + Existing Exports → Larger Global Opportunity: Nearly 40% of revenue already comes from exports, while new capacity is intended partly to deepen international penetration.

IPO coming at 12.5 PE

items.title: RT Swapnil Srivastav: 🚨 Indian logistics companies have found the perfect scam: steal from D2C brands and let the customer take the blame. Here’s ...
items.description_html:
RT Swapnil Srivastav
🚨 Indian logistics companies have found the perfect scam: steal from D2C brands and let the customer take the blame.

Here’s how it works:

→ Prepaid order gets “cancelled” without the customer or brand knowing

→ Brand gets charged two-way delivery fees for an order nobody cancelled

→ Small items get shipped back in oversized boxes to inflate the RTO cost

→ Customer calls in confused: “I never cancelled this, I was waiting for it”

The brand loses the product, the shipping cost, the RTO cost, and the customer relationship. In one transaction.

Every D2C founder in India has lived this. Not once. On repeat.

And the wildest part? This is a multi thousand crore leak across the industry and almost nobody is building to fix it. 🤷🏻‍♂️

items.description_html:
RT Gregory Brew
With benefit of hindsight, it does appear as though Iran was pushing its luck back in July, when it resumed attacks on shipping in the southern route.

The Iranian calculation was that it was necessary to maintain effective control over Hormuz flows.

The result: the MOU is dead, the blockade is back in place, and the US is succeeding (to a partial, but notable extent) at reopening the strait without another deal.

Perhaps the status quo swings back in Iran's favor, but right now this looks like a miscalculation to me.


Gregory Brew: Agree

Iran is pushing its luck in Hormuz--there's clearly a belief that US is deterred, that Trump doesn't want to go back to war, and there's scope for continuing the war-time use of force to govern flows through the strait.

US response is very clear: bombings will continue

طهران | 27 أغسطس 2026

اجتمع معالي الشيخ محمد بن عبدالرحمن بن جاسم آل ثاني، رئيس مجلس الوزراء وزير الخارجية، اليوم في طهران، مع سعادة السيد عباس عراقجي، وزير الخارجية بالجمهورية الإسلامية الإيرانية.

جرى خلال الاجتماع، استعراض آخر تطورات الأوضاع في المنطقة، والجهود المبذولة لخفض التصعيد وتهيئة الظروف الملائمة للحوار، بما يسهم في تعزيز الأمن والاستقرار الإقليميين.

كما تطرق الاجتماع إلى المناقشات الجارية بشأن الإطار المرحلي المقترح، الذي يتضمن إنشاء ممر ملاحي مؤقت مشترك عبر مضيق هرمز، والاتفاق على تنفيذ مشروع مشترك لتطهير المضيق من الألغام.

وشدد معالي رئيس مجلس الوزراء وزير الخارجية، خلال الاجتماع، على ضرورة احترام سيادة دول الجوار، واحترام حرية الملاحة، مؤكداً أهمية مواصلة الجهود الدبلوماسية لخفض التصعيد ومعالجة الخلافات عبر الحوار.

من جانبه، أعرب سعادة وزير الخارجية الإيراني عن شكره وتقديره لدولة قطر على استمرار مساعيها وجهودها الدبلوماسية الرامية إلى خفض التصعيد ودعم الحوار.

items.title: Gaja Capital is raising funds through an IPO primarily to meet its own sponsor commitments in its AIF structures, including offshore vehicles. A key q...
items.description_html:
Gaja Capital is raising funds through an IPO primarily to meet its own sponsor commitments in its AIF structures, including offshore vehicles.

A key question is — if the existing sponsor capital has already increased by nearly 20% in the last year, why does the company need to raise fresh capital from public investors to invest further in these high-risk, illiquid assets?

Interestingly, around 85% of Gaja’s income comes from management fees and carried interest, while income from sponsor commitments contributes only about 10%.

This raises a fundamental question: a significant portion of the fresh issue proceeds is being deployed toward an activity that currently contributes a relatively small share of revenue.

Moreover, carried interest is dependent on successful exits and realisation of investment gains. Until portfolio investments are monetised, the carried interest recorded in financial statements may not necessarily translate into actual cash inflows.

The key investor question is whether the additional sponsor commitments will create enough incremental value through future fee income and carry generation to justify the capital being raised

items.title: Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20% The vaccine is not a prev...
items.description_html:
Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20%

The vaccine is not a preventive vaccine like a COVID shot. It's made after patient already has cancer. Each dose is built individually for that patient from the mutations found in their own tumour — you sequence the tumour, find the mutated proteins unique to it ("neoantigens"), and make an mRNA shot that teaches the immune system to hunt cells carrying those specific mutations.

It's the first proof the idea works. Neoantigen vaccines have been a theoretical hope in oncology for years, but this is the first randomised Phase 3 trial designed to definitively prove the benefit.

If the mechanism is real, it's platform technology — the same pipeline could in principle be pointed at lung, kidney, bladder cancers. One analyst noted the results also read positively for the vaccine's ongoing studies in other cancer types. That optionality is what "holy grail" headlines are reaching for.

items.description_html:
🚨 C2C’s auditor has issued a qualified opinion and flagged multiple serious financial and compliance concerns:

1️⃣ Liquidity & Going Concern Risk:
The company is facing a liquidity crisis, with statutory dues unpaid due to lack of funds. Recovery from trade receivables remains uncertain, while operations are heavily dependent on short-term promoter funding. The auditor has raised doubt over C2C’s ability to continue as a going concern. Liquidation Risk

2️⃣ CSR Payments Not Cleared:
CSR expenses were recognised through cheques, creating a book overdraft. However, the cheques were not presented for payment. The auditor noted that the CSR obligation is discharged only when the payment is actually cleared.

3️⃣ Statutory Dues Pending:
Undisputed statutory payments remain unpaid. No provision has been made for possible interest or penalties. Delays in filing statutory returns and weak internal controls were also highlighted.

4️⃣ Labour Code Impact Not Assessed:
The company has not quantified the potential impact of new labour regulations on gratuity, provident fund, wages and other employee benefits.

5️⃣ FEMA Compliance Issues:
Overseas receivables remain unrealised beyond RBI timelines. Applications for regularisation are pending, SOFTEX registration is yet to be approved, and possible penalties have not been provided for.

items.title: P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/E...
items.description_html:
P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/EBITDA. I had demonstrated this through correlation analysis in an earlier investor memo.

The chart below tracks the P/B ratio (blue line) of the Nifty Smallcap 100 Index against the 25th percentile of its trailing 5-year P/B range (orange line). In simple terms, when the blue line falls below the orange line, the current valuation is in the lowest quartile of the past five years.

Since P/B is broadly proportional to ROE, the structural improvement in index ROE—from ~8–12% in the previous decade to ~15% currently—has led to a gradual upward shift in the orange line over time.

Notably, for the first time since the COVID crash, the current P/B has moved below this 25th percentile threshold. Historically, similar instances—during the 2011–2013 downturn, Q1 2016 correction, and the COVID crash—have been followed by strong returns over the subsequent 1–3 years.

This does not imply that markets have bottomed, nor does it guarantee short-term gains. In an event-driven environment, especially with geopolitical risks such as an escalation in war, markets could decline further by 10–20%.

However, what can be said with a reasonably high degree of confidence is that forward-looking returns over a 1–3 year horizon from such valuation levels have historically been better than average.

items.description_html: In my experience, this is probably the first time the Mid & Small cap indices have outperformed the Nifty 50 during a crisis time. It's also extremely rare to see the Mid & Small cap indices (avg of the two) beating the Nifty 50 near the bottom of the cycle. Their avg CAGR has outperformed during the last two tough years as well as all the below trailing years. I am not that surprised as their balance sheet, P&L and cash flow quality has substantially improved post COVID. I believe the biggest multi-baggers will emerge from this space as the earnings growth differential will be significant going forward. Because of the quality differential today vs during pre-COVID period, I would be surprised if their valuations correct to levels seen during the previous crashes. We probably have the best corporate quality and least stressed financials currently compared to any other previous big crisis.

Small cap has an exceptional earnings from Kiri Ind with 5000 cr plus (vs 177 cr year ago) which skews the growth much higher than normal. If you remove that, the wtd avg growth is 14.9%. Median growth reduces influence of such outliers or exceptional items and hence gives a better directional picture. Over all growth is good but nothing exceptional. I believe we should see much improved growth in the Mar'26 quarter as sharp pick up in economic activity (as covered in my last memo) started in the month of December 2025.

items.title: As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/Mar...
items.description_html:
As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/March trough—are not an exception; they are a recurring feature of market cycles. Just as consistently, these phases have been followed by sharp recoveries once the market establishes a bottom in February or March.
Current sentiment is such that investors are overly focused on the negatives, making the environment appear so foggy that positives have become invisible. This fog, as always, will eventually lift.

While market bottoms and the depth of drawdowns can never be predicted, it is highly probable that market levels a few months from now will be disproportionately higher. Unfortunately, short-term declines are unsettling for investors, causing many to step aside and miss the eventual strong upswing.

In hindsight, this phase will look like an obvious opportunity. But while living through it, investors see only risks and landmines—never the runway for the next flight
